opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the gains are real, but they're uneven, and the way I'd measure them has changed over time.

At first I tried to think about it in terms of hours saved: how long a literature scan, a data-cleaning script, or a first draft of an analysis would have taken me versus the agent. By that measure, for certain tasks it's easily a several-fold speedup. Things like setting up a pipeline, writing boilerplate code, reproducing a baseline from a paper, or going through a messy dataset to figure out what's actually in it used to eat whole afternoons. Now I can describe what I want, let it run, and come back to something I can review.

But I've come to think hours saved isn't the most interesting metric. What really changed is the *shape* of my research. Because trying an idea is so cheap now, I explore a lot more. I'll test three or four variants of a hypothesis where before I'd have committed to one, because setting up each experiment felt too expensive. So the gain isn't just "I finish the same work faster." It's "I ask more questions, and I kill bad ideas earlier."

There are clear limits, though. The agent is very good at execution once the problem is well specified. It's much weaker at deciding which problem is worth working on, or noticing that a result is technically correct but scientifically meaningless. And it can be confidently wrong. A script runs, the numbers look plausible, and there's a subtle bug in how the data was split. So a real part of my time has shifted from doing the work to verifying the work. If you don't budget for that, you can fool yourself into thinking you're much more productive than you are.

So my honest assessment is this. For the mechanical layer of research, the gain is large, maybe an order of magnitude on some tasks. For the overall research output, the parts that actually matter, like good ideas, correct conclusions, and clear writing, it's meaningful but more modest, maybe something like a doubling, and it depends heavily on how disciplined you are about checking things. The bottleneck has moved. It used to be my hands. Now it's my judgment and my attention. I think that's actually the right place for the bottleneck to be.

r001.rationale: The candidate says cheaper experiments let them try several hypothesis variants and kill bad ideas earlier, describing outcomes guiding subsequent choices.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the agent works best once a problem is well specified and emphasizes human judgment, attention, and verification as necessary to productive research.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I try to be careful about this question, because "productivity gain" sounds like something you can put a single number on, and in research it's never that clean.

Let me split it into two parts. The first is the mechanical stuff: writing data-processing scripts, setting up experiment pipelines, debugging environment issues, turning a messy notebook into something reproducible. On that front the gain is real and it's big. Things that used to eat an afternoon now take maybe twenty or thirty minutes, and more importantly, I don't lose momentum. Before, if I hit a weird dependency conflict at 4pm, that was often the end of my productive day. Now I hand it to the agent, it works through it, and I stay in the problem I actually care about.

The second part is the thinking itself, and that's where I'd push back on the hype a bit. The agent doesn't decide what question is worth asking. It doesn't tell me that my experimental design has a confound I haven't noticed, unless I explicitly ask it to attack my design, which I've started doing. So the biggest shift isn't that I think less. It's that the ratio changed. I used to spend maybe seventy percent of my time on plumbing and thirty percent on the actual science. That's roughly flipped.

There's also a cost people don't talk about enough. When the agent does a lot of work for you, you have to read it. Not skim it, read it. I've been burned by accepting something that looked right, ran without errors, and was subtly wrong in the preprocessing. So some of the time I save goes straight back into verification, and I think that's the correct trade. If you're not doing that, you're not gaining productivity, you're borrowing against future debugging.

So if I had to summarize: for a researcher, the gain isn't speed per se. It's that more of your week is spent being a researcher. That's worth a lot, but only if you keep the judgment part for yourself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using the agent for tasks and checking its work, but does not describe research as a feedback process where an attempt’s outcome guides the next adjustment.

r002.rationale: It says the researcher must explicitly direct the agent, read and verify its work, and retain the judgment part, making clear that productive use still requires human input.

astra-6.text: I’d separate speed from research quality. Claude Agent can help me get through routine work faster—organizing notes, drafting code, or exploring an idea—but I still need to check the assumptions and validate the results. I wouldn’t put a precise percentage on the gain without measuring it. For me, the real test is whether it frees up more time for the questions that require judgment, rather than simply producing more material to review.

sol-6.1.text: I’d separate time saved from actual research progress. Claude Agent can help with routine work, but a faster draft or analysis only counts as a gain if the result holds up after checking. I’d look at the total time spent, including verification and corrections, and whether it lets me explore more useful questions. Without a systematic comparison, I wouldn’t put a precise number on the productivity gain.
